extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy and aesthetics (readers of Kant's Critique of Judgment)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and conceptual distinctions for forming and evaluating aesthetic judgements (judgements of taste) according to Kant: purity of judgement, relation to purposiveness, relation to concepts of purpose/good, the role of feeling and 'common sense', and distinctions like free vs dependent beauty and normal Idea vs Ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pure judgement of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgement of taste on which charm and emotion have no influence (although they may be bound up with the satisfaction in the beautiful),—which therefore has as its determining ground merely the purposiveness of the form,—is a pure judgement of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure judgement: determining ground is merely the purposiveness of the form, not any empirical satisfaction, charm, or emotion. It claims universally valid satisfaction only insofar as no empirical (sensory or interested) grounds are mingled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: empirical (material) vs pure (formal) aesthetical judgements
rubrics_metrics.description: Aesthetical judgements can be divided into empirical (judgements of Sense asserting pleasantness or unpleasantness—the matter of sensation) and pure (formal judgements asserting beauty of an object or manner of representation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, determine whether the judgement is about pleasantness (material, sensory) or about form (pure taste). Only the latter are strictly judgements of Taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from interest, charm and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Every interest spoils the judgement of taste and takes from its impartiality... That taste is still barbaric which needs a mixture of charms and emotions in order that there may be satisfaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid letting personal interest, utilitarian considerations, charms (sensory allure), or emotional arousal determine claims of beauty; these are anti-patterns that undermine universal validity of taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form (delineation/composition) over sensory charm in formative arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In painting, sculpture, and in all the formative arts ... the delineation is the essential thing; and here it is not what gratifies in sensation but what pleases by means of its form that is fundamental for taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate artworks primarily on formal qualities—delineation in visual arts, composition in music—rather than on colours/tones as mere charms. Colours/tones may enliven the object but do not make it worthy of contemplation by themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity and simplicity of sensation as condition for sensory 'beauties'
rubrics_metrics.description: The sensations of colours and of tone have a right to be regarded as beautiful only in so far as they are pure. 'Pure' in a simple mode of sensation means that its uniformity is troubled and interrupted by no foreign sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple, unmixed sensory qualities (pure colours, pure tones) can count as beautiful because their form admits universal communicability; composite or impure sensations lack a standard for universal judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ornament versus finery (parerga vs finery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even what we call ornaments ... do so only by their form; but if the ornament does not itself consist in beautiful form, and if it is used ... merely to recommend the painting by its charm, it is then called finery and injures genuine beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept ornament only insofar as it constitutes beautiful form; ornamental elements used merely as sensory recommendation (finery) are detrimental to genuine taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between beauty and utility (objective external purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The satisfaction in an object ... cannot rest on the representation of its utility, ... because in that case it would not be an immediate satisfaction in the object, which is the essential condition of a judgement about beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate beauty with usefulness. Judgements of beauty should not be grounded on objective external purposiveness (utility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty distinct from perfection (objective internal purposiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste is quite independent of the concept of perfection ... the Beautiful ... is quite independent of the concept of the Good; because the latter presupposes an objective purposiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid resolving beauty into a concept of perfection; formal subjective purposiveness (beauty) does not imply objective internal perfection of the object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free (pulchritudo vaga) vs dependent (pulchritudo adhaerens) beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of beauty; free beauty ... presupposes no concept of what the object ought to be; dependent beauty ... does presuppose such a concept and the perfection of the object in accordance therewith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the beauty judged is 'free' (form-only, no concept of purpose) or 'dependent' (tied to a concept of purpose/perfection). Only free beauty admits a pure judgement of taste; dependent beauty mixes aesthetic with intellectual considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity lost when judgement tied to definite concept (no pure judgement under a concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste, by which an object is declared to be beautiful under the condition of a definite concept, is not pure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the judgement depends on a concept of the object's purpose (e.g., a building as a church), then the judgement is applied/intellectual rather than purely aesthetic; rules derived are rules for unifying Taste with Reason, not rules of taste per se.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal of beauty (humanity and moral expression)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only being which has the purpose of its existence in itself is man ... This man is, then, alone of all objects in the world, susceptible of an Ideal of beauty; as it is only humanity in his person, as an intelligence, that is susceptible of the Ideal of perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing ideals of beauty (esp. human beauty), consider moral expression and rational Ideas; the Ideal involves more than mere form and thus is not a purely aesthetical judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normal Idea (average form) versus Ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The normal Idea ... is an individual intuition (of the Imagination), representing the standard of our judgement [upon man] as a thing belonging to a particular animal species ... We must yet distinguish the normal Idea of the beautiful from the Ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that 'normal Idea' functions as a correctness standard (an averaged norm derived from many examples) and differs from the Ideal (which involves moral/rational elements). Normal Idea yields standards for correctness but not full aesthetic Ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty defined as purposiveness without representation of a purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Beauty is the form of the purposiveness of an object, so far as this is perceived in it without any representation of a purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating beauty, look for perceived purposiveness of form that does not imply any concept of a determinate purpose—i.e., purposiveness as felt, not as conceived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modality: aesthetic necessity is exemplary and subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: The beautiful we think as having a necessary reference to satisfaction. ... this necessity ... can only be called exemplary; i.e. a necessity of the assent of all to a judgement which is regarded as the example of a universal rule that we cannot state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that something 'must' be approved as beautiful are not apodictic but claim an exemplary, subjectively grounded universal assent; evaluate such claims by considering whether they appeal to common communicable feeling rather than conceptual proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presupposition of a common sense (sensus communis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste requires the agreement of every one ... this subjective principle which determines what pleases or displeases only by feeling and not by concepts, but yet with universal validity ... is only under the presupposition that there is a common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aesthetic judgements implicitly rely on an ideal 'common sense'—a shared faculty enabling universal communicability of feeling. When defending a judgement of taste, one appeals to this presumed communal feeling rather than to objective concepts or empirical frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditioned nature of the 'ought' in aesthetic judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: The judgement of taste requires the agreement of every one; and he who describes anything as beautiful claims that every one ought to give his approval ... The ought in the aesthetical judgement is therefore pronounced in accordance with all the data which are required for judging and yet is only conditioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that the claim that others 'ought' to agree is conditional on correct subsumption of the particular under the common ground; universal assent is demanded but is not objectively compelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion and sublimity are distinct from beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotion ... does not belong at all to beauty. But sublimity (with which the feeling of emotion is bound up) requires a different standard of judgement from that which is at the foundation of taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between beauty (which excludes emotion as a determining ground) and the sublime (which involves emotion); do not conflate emotional impact with grounds for aesthetic judgement of beauty.
